newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Rugby union-Carnival atmosphere follows Fiji win.
newsitem.headline: Rugby union-Carnival atmosphere follows Fiji win.

text.p: A carnival atmosphere pervaded the Hong Kong Stadium as thousands of rugby fans watched Fiji lift the World Cup on Sunday.
It was the climax to three days of partying as 24 teams fought it out for the Melrose Cup, named after the Scottish club who invented the abridged form of rugby.
An ecstatic Fijian team brandished their trophy while the crowd roared its approval, and toasted them vigorously after their 24-21 victory over South Africa in the final.
The event incorporated the annual Hong Kong Rugby Sevens, and in keeping with the spirit of previous competitions, there was as much happening off the pitch as on it.
Streakers, stubbly nuns, Viking warriors and Elvis Presley impersonators enlivened the terraces, in marked contrast to the more low-key event at Murrayfield in Scotland in 1993.
Governor Chris Patten presented the cup to the victorious team before Hong Kong tenor Warren Mok sang "Amazing Grace" and "Auld Lang Syne" and the specators linked hands.
The closing ceremony was in many ways the end of an era for Hong Kong, and the start of a new one.
The territory reverts to Chinese sovereignty on July 1, after more than 150 years of British rule.
Patten, an avowed rugby fan, was presiding over his last Hong Kong Sevens as governor, and next year's tournament will be played under the auspices of chief executive Tung Chee-hwa.
Tung made an appearance over the weekend, telling reporters it was important for Hong Kong to host major international events.

China's People's Liberation Army, which takes over the responsibility of defending the territory on July 1, showed its commitment to rugby last week when it defeated its counterparts from the British armed forces in a game of 10-a-side rugby.
The annual Hong Kong Sevens is a cash bonanza for the territory, with an estimated 15,000 visitors expected to spend HK$7,000 ($900) each during their stay.
